81312.subject: The $PEARL Bear Case
81312.body:
View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/eaa70932-7ce4-467e-b338-a662ed575d6a/0xR_NL_Banner_Heading_Wordmark.jpg?t=1776775276)
Caption: 

I’ll just go ahead and say it. I don’t like [Pearl](https://app.blockworks.com/projects/pearl-ai). I am a PEARL bear and will continue to be, even if it runs to $10B. The thing is, its fundamentals are just objectively bad, and I am a fundamental investor. If you are a PEARL holder solely for the narrative and the short term, I understand. If you hold it for the fundamentals, you are wrong. (And if you hate that I said that, don’t worry, we have a full Pearl research piece dropping soon).

But let me steelman the bull case before I give my bear case.

Pearl’s [Proof of Useful Work](https://pearlresearch.ai/research/blog/proof-of-useful-work) is a genuinely innovative and novel security model. As it stands, Bitcoin mining burns electricity on hashes that serve no other purpose, while Pearl uses the matrix multiplications from AI training and inference to secure its blockchain. Also, Bitcoin’s block rewards most likely won’t cover rising mining costs, especially after the 2028 halving, which is why many miners are already switching to AI. But switching means giving up mining, since Bitcoin ASICs can’t run AI workloads. On Pearl, the same GPUs can serve AI customers and mine at the same time.

An AI provider can mine PEARL on the GPUs it already has, without building dedicated infrastructure, and the [proposed FP8 upgrade](https://pearlresearch.ai/Pearl_Whitepaper.pdf) aligns mining even more closely with modern AI workloads. AI revenue pays for the machines, and PEARL becomes extra income. That’s the best answer to the sell-pressure argument: a miner whose GPU is already paid for doesn’t have to dump coins to cover power.

On top of this, the team is stacked. It is built by [Omri Weinstein](https://www.linkedin.com/in/omri-weinstein-27468819/?isSelfProfile=false) (ex-Nvidia/Microsoft/Vast Data, Professor of CS at Hebrew University, and on leave from Columbia) and [Ilan Komargodski](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ilankomargodski/) (cryptographer at NTT Research and Professor of CS at Hebrew University). PEARL’s was also a fair launch (per the team) with no VC rounds, team allocation, or unlock cliff (though roughly a third of today’s circulating supply was mined in the first six days, and we don’t know how much of that went to the team).

Then there’s the monetary premium case. Like BTC, PEARL has no cash flows, so its value comes from a monetary premium (what people will pay to hold a scarce, neutral, PoW-secured asset). PEARL has a 2.1B hard cap, and since AI customers cover much of miners’ costs, its security doesn’t have to shrink as issuance does. Dilution is also front-loaded (~85% this year, ~33% next year, and ~18% the year after), so the market is arguably pricing the worst year right now. And the momentum is c

81310.body:
The Atlas

Автор: GenAI Works

Welcome back! Five major banks are finding AI agents inside customer accounts, NVIDIA shipped two products that work against each other, PHP took down sites worldwide, and two labs publicly disagreed about what Claude actually is.  In today's Atlas Newsletter: NVIDIA is now competing with its own data centers: 768GB on a desk, and compute trays that assemble in five minutes instead of two hours. Something is logging into US bank accounts: Not a hacker. An agent with the customer’s own password, and the fraud controls never fire. Two PHP bugs took websites offline worldwide: The FBI’s advice is patch now or take systems offline, and PHP wasn’t the only one this week. Two AI labs just disagreed about what Claude is: Microsoft says design the inner life out. Anthropic says nobody knows enough to try. PS: Want to collaborate with the biggest GTM engine and distribution moat for AI companies? You can feature your tool with us and reach millions. Something is logging into U.S. bank accounts It is not a hacker. It is an AI agent, using the customer’s own password, because the customer handed it over. Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and Citi are all dealing with it, per Axios.  Some agents have been tracked calling into call centers. Others took actions that don’t map to anything the user asked for. One executive called the situation horrifying. The mechanism is what makes it hard.  When an agent logs in as you, the session is indistinguishable from you. Every fraud control the bank built stays silent, because nothing about the login looks wrong. Morgan Stanley has started blocking third-party agents. JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are restricting them. Chase’s line: don’t give your credentials to anyone. Most banks are landing on read-only access, which is the right fix.  The agent sees your balances and can’t move money, because the permission sits in the API rather than in the agent’s judgment. Same model already granted to tools like Quicken. This is the same argument Microsoft made this week when it shipped Guardian Agents.  Its security chief put it plainly: frontier models cannot be trusted, not because they’re malicious but because they’re unpredictable, and they get handed the data and tools that matter most.  Satya Nadella’s framing was to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.
